questions.q: Who did Nixon’s 1968 campaign target with coded appeals instead of explicit labels?
a: Voters the book calls “nonracist racists”
White voters who supported civil rights
Black voters in northern cities
Recent immigrants without party loyalty
questions.why: Lesson 1 says Nixon avoided the words black and white to reach people with subtly racist views.

questions.q: What reassuring promise did Nixon use in ads showing civil rights protests?
a: That there would be order in the United States
That taxes would be cut for everyone
That segregation would end within a decade
That every citizen would get a job
questions.why: Lesson 1 quotes the pledge for order, which appealed to voters unsettled by protest imagery.

questions.q: How did Reagan use the story of Linda Taylor?
a: He linked a rare welfare fraud case to black people generally
He praised her as an example of entrepreneurial success
He used her case to argue for stronger welfare programs
He cited her to criticize white suburban voters
questions.why: Lesson 1 says Reagan presented an unusual fraud case as typical and exaggerated the amount involved.

questions.q: Why might arrest statistics make black neighborhoods look more dangerous?
a: Heavier police presence there produces more arrests
Residents there report crimes less often
Those neighborhoods have no other recorded data
Police keep separate records for white areas
questions.why: Lesson 2 says more policing driven by perceived crime can itself inflate the number of arrests.

questions.q: What does the summary say about drunk driving compared with so-called urban black violence?
a: Drunk driving kills more people but is not counted as violent crime
Drunk driving is less deadly than cocaine use
Drunk driving is treated as the most serious violent crime
Drunk driving deaths are lower than inner-city homicide
questions.why: Lesson 2 notes that drunk driving causes more deaths yet is excluded from violent crime statistics.
